newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin creates tax commission to ease wage crisis. [corrected 08:20 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin creates tax commission to ease wage crisis. [corrected 08:20 gmt]

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin on Friday announced the creation of a special commission to improve tax collection to provide cash to pay off a huge backlog of wages to state sector workers, servicemen and pensioners.

In a brief radio address highlighting two serious problems facing the Russian economy -- poor tax collection and mounting wage arrears -- Yeltsin said the need to create the commission reflected the "extraordinary situation" in Russia.

"Payment of salaries and pensions is not only a question of politics and economy. It is also a question of conscience (corrects from "morale" to "conscience")," he said, speaking clearly in an address apparently recorded in the Barvikha sanatorium where he is getting ready for heart surgery.
"I may assure pensioners and the workers of budget sphere, policemen and servicemen. Pensions and salaries will be paid. I, as president, am confident of it."

Dismal tax collection has curbed the government's ability to fulfil its spending plans and cast a shadow over the possible approval of the 1997 budget, which the lower house of parliament was debating.
Deputies are expected to reject the draft, which envisages a tight deficit of 3.3 percent of gross domestic product.
Yeltsin, 65, said on Thursday that big business tax dodgers meant problems with state spending.

"Students, teachers, the military and other workers in the state sphere are not receiving wages because a number of big enterprises are literally taking the finances of the country by the throat and refusing to pay taxes," Yeltsin said.
That is unlikely to appease his Communist opponents, who dominate the State Duma and are set to lead demands that the government revise its austere 1997 budget.
If parliament rejects the plan, the government has 20 days to come up with new proposals.
Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov said the government was breaking promises Yeltsin made during his re-election campaign.
"The budget doesn't correspond to those main messages which were in the (government) statement when (parliament) confirmed its appointment," said Zyuganov, the runner-up in July's vote.
The Communists and their close allies have more than 200 of the Duma's 450 seats. Even the party set up by Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, Our Home is Russia, wants the spending plans reviewed.
Chernomyrdin has already said he will look for more money for the military.
But the queue for cash does not end there, leaving the government trying to make ends meet to keep its promises to the International Monetary Fund, which helps bankroll any shortfall.
A delegation from the fund is due in Moscow next week to discuss economic performances and decide whether to release the next tranche of a three-year $10 billion loan.
